history.rationale: Starting with a standard, well-regularized baseline with moderate depth and learning rate to establish initial benchmark performance.
Trial 1 reached 0.578; testing a shallower tree (depth 3) with higher min_child_weight to reduce noise fitting on rare positive cases.
Testing higher interaction depth (max_depth 6) with conservative feature subsampling and higher min_child_weight to test if complex interactions exist without overfitting.
Trial 3 showed max_depth 6 reached 0.5826; testing max_depth 5 to see if intermediate depth provides an even better bias-variance trade-off.
Testing max_depth 4 with the strong regularization parameters from Trial 4 to confirm whether depth 5 is indeed superior to depth 4.
With max_depth 5 performing best, testing higher min_child_weight (8) to see if requiring more samples per leaf improves precision on this 7% positive dataset.
Trial 6 jumped to 0.5888 with min_child_weight 8; testing min_child_weight 10 to see if even higher leaf sample constraint continues this upward trend.
Comparing min_child_weight 8 (0.5888) and 10 (0.5877), testing 9 to pinpoint the exact optimal threshold.
Now that min_child_weight 9 unlocked 0.5908, testing max_depth 6 with min_child_weight 9 to see if deeper trees can exploit this higher leaf constraint.
Testing max_depth 4 with min_child_weight 9 to confirm whether depth 5 is strictly optimal under this leaf weight constraint.
Evaluating whether increasing feature subsampling to 0.7 improves diversity and feature coverage while keeping depth 5 and min_child_weight 9.
Trial 8 (colsample 0.6) outperformed 0.7; testing colsample 0.5 to see if more aggressive feature decorrelation boosts PR-AUC further.
With colsample centered at 0.6, testing higher subsample (0.85) to reduce row sampling variance on rare positive events.
Subsample 0.85 dropped to 0.5814, showing row regularization is essential; testing subsample 0.65 to see if lower subsampling beats 0.75.
Subsample 0.75 is optimal; now testing stronger L1/L2 regularization (alpha 0.8, lambda 8.0) to penalize noisy leaf weights on the 7% positive target.
Testing slightly milder regularization (alpha 0.2, lambda 3.0) relative to Trial 8 to find the regularization peak.
Halving learning rate to 0.02 and doubling estimators to 280 with the best regularized depth-5 architecture to reduce shrinkage variance.
Testing if 140 estimators in Trial 8 slightly overfit by reducing tree count to 110 at learning rate 0.04.
With 110 estimators underfitting at 0.5863, testing 160 estimators to see if additional boosting rounds past 140 improve performance.
Since colsample 0.6 (0.59086) and 0.7 (0.59007) both performed strongly, testing 0.65 to interpolate the exact optimum.
Testing slightly higher learning rate (0.05) with 120 estimators to verify whether faster convergence improves the decision boundary.
Evaluating lr 0.035 with 160 estimators to see if slightly more gradual gradient steps improve on lr 0.04.
Testing subsample 0.78 between 0.75 and 0.85 to see if slight increase in sample exposure sharpens leaf probability estimates.
Subsample 0.78 degraded performance, testing 0.72 to see if slightly lower subsample than 0.75 offers stronger regularization.
Evaluating slightly reduced L2 regularization (reg_lambda 4.0 vs 5.0) while keeping optimal L1 alpha at 0.5.
With reg_lambda 4 underperforming 5 (0.5900 vs 0.59086), testing reg_lambda 6 to check the upper side of the L2 regularization curvature.
Holding reg_lambda at the proven optimal value of 5.0, testing reg_alpha 0.4 to fine-tune L1 feature selection penalty.
With reg_alpha 0.4 boosting PR-AUC to 0.5925, testing reg_alpha 0.3 to see if slightly looser L1 sparsity improves further.
Comparing reg_alpha 0.4 (0.5925) and 0.5 (0.5909), testing 0.45 to hone in on the exact optimal L1 regularization.
Exploring directly adjacent to top-performing Trial 27 (0.5925) by testing reg_alpha 0.38 to check if a fractionally lower L1 penalty achieves even higher validation PR-AUC.

history.rationale: Initial baseline trial with moderate depth, standard subsampling, and conservative learning rate to establish a baseline PR-AUC.
Testing lower depth (3) and higher min_child_weight (5) with more trees against Trial 1 baseline to see if reducing model complexity reduces overfitting on rare positive cases.
Testing higher tree depth (6) with lower min_child_weight and feature subsampling (0.6) to see if deeper feature interactions improve ranking over Trial 1.
Given that depth 6 severely underperformed (0.5646 vs 0.5797 in Trial 1), testing very shallow trees (depth 2) to evaluate whether minimal depth with more boosting steps prevents overfitting.
With depth 2 (0.5740) and depth 3 (0.5774) both trailing depth 4 (0.5797), testing depth 5 with moderate child weight and regularization to find the peak tree complexity.
Trial 5 set a new best (0.5813) at depth 5; testing slightly higher min_child_weight (6) to curb minority-class leaf variance with slightly lower learning rate.
Trial 6 showed min_child_weight=6 was worse than 4; testing min_child_weight=3 at depth 5 to see if finer leaf partitioning improves PR-AUC.
Fixing min_child_weight=4 and depth=5 from best Trial 5, testing higher colsample_bytree (0.85) to assess if seeing more features per tree improves decision boundaries.
Comparing colsample 0.85 (0.5807) and 0.75 (0.5813), testing lower colsample (0.65) to see if decorrelating trees further improves performance.
Keeping best colsample (0.75), testing higher subsample (0.9) to provide more training instances per tree given the rare positive class.
Since subsample 0.9 dropped performance, testing subsample 0.70 to test whether stronger sample bagging improves generalization on minority cases.
Subsample 0.7 improved score to 0.5817 over 0.8 (0.5813); testing subsample 0.65 to explore if lower sample correlation further enhances performance.
Trial 12 showed a massive leap to 0.5891 at subsample=0.65; testing subsample=0.60 to see if heavier bagging continues to boost PR-AUC.
With subsample 0.65 delivering 0.5891 in Trial 12, testing higher L2 regularization (reg_lambda=3.0) to prevent weight inflation on noisy minority signals.
Trial 14 showed reg_lambda=3.0 degraded PR-AUC to 0.5790; testing lower reg_lambda=0.8 to see if less shrinkage allows better minority class separation.
With reg_lambda=1.5 proven superior to 0.8 and 3.0, testing higher L1 sparsity (reg_alpha=0.3) to filter out uninformative features.
Testing lower L1 regularization (reg_alpha=0.03 vs 0.10 in Trial 12) to see if preserving minor non-zero feature weights improves rank ordering.
Given the solid performance at lr=0.04 (Trial 12: 0.5891), testing lower learning rate (0.03) with proportionately more trees (180) to smooth convergence.
Testing slightly higher learning rate (0.045) and fewer estimators (130) compared to Trial 12 to see if faster boosting reaches peak PR-AUC before noise accumulates.
Keeping the optimal lr=0.04 and subsample=0.65 from Trial 12, testing if allowing 20 additional trees (160) captures further minority signals.
Trial 20 reached a new peak (0.5900) at 160 estimators; testing 175 estimators to check whether PR-AUC continues climbing before peaking.
With 175 estimators achieving 0.5910 in Trial 21, pushing to 190 estimators to map out the peak of the boosting curve.
Trial 22 showed another gain at 190 estimators (0.5915); testing 210 estimators to check if the optimum lies slightly higher.
With n_estimators=190 established as optimal in Trial 22, fine-tuning subsample from 0.65 to 0.67 to pin down the exact bagging fraction.
Trial 24 jumped to 0.5924 with subsample=0.67; testing subsample=0.69 to see if the peak lies between 0.67 and 0.70.
Trial 25 made a major jump to 0.5956 at subsample=0.69; testing subsample=0.71 to see if slightly higher sample coverage further improves ranking.
With 0.71 dropping sharply to 0.5817 and 0.69 reaching 0.5956, testing subsample=0.68 to test the stable basin around 0.69.
Since subsample 0.69 yielded 0.5956 and 0.71 dropped, testing exactly 0.70 at 190 estimators to determine if 0.69 or 0.70 holds the absolute peak.
With subsample=0.69 establishing the top mark in Trial 25 (0.5956), testing 180 estimators to see if slightly earlier stopping improves generalization further.
Since 180 estimators scored 0.5935 and 190 reached 0.5956, testing 195 estimators to determine if the optimum peaks just past 190.
